# renv for Package Management {#sec-renv} A project that worked in January may fail in July because a dependency changed underneath it, and a failure is the easy case, because it is loud and gets fixed. The dangerous case is the one where nothing fails: the code still runs, the report still renders, and one of the numbers is different, because a default changed or a tie is now broken the other way. The analyst who re-runs the old analysis and gets a slightly different table has no way, without a record of what was installed the first time, to tell a genuine correction from a silent regression. `renv` supplies that record: it pins the exact package versions a project uses in a lockfile, so that any discrepancy becomes attributable rather than mysterious. ::: {.bookepigraph} ```{=latex} \begin{flushright}\small ``` *Controlling complexity is the essence of computer programming.* [Brian W. Kernighan and P. J. Plauger]{.smallcaps}, *Software Tools* (1976) ```{=latex} \end{flushright} ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Where this chapter sits: `renv` pins the R packages in the Environment band, which runs under every stage of the analysis.](08-renv_files/figure-html/fig-renv-pipeline-1.png){#fig-renv-pipeline fig-align='center' fig-alt='Diagram of the analysis pipeline: six stages in order (Plan, Acquire, Wrangle, Analyze, Report, Share) above two bands that run under every stage (Version control and Environment). Highlighted for this chapter: Environment.' width=100%} ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note title='In this chapter'} **Reading time.** About 20 minutes. **You'll need.** @sec-git-solo for commits and tags. The compendium layout the chapter mentions in passing is assembled in full in @sec-rrtools, later in this part. The chapter calls every `renv` function with its namespace (`renv::snapshot()`), so it needs no `library()` call; install the package once with `install.packages("renv")`. **You'll be able to.** - Initialize `renv` in a new or existing project and state which of its files are committed. - Choose between `renv::snapshot()` and `renv::restore()` from the report of `renv::status()`. - Read a lockfile to find the version and source of any package, including the commit of a GitHub package. - Find the packages the dependency scan misses, and audit the lockfile before tagging a submission. **Outline.** - [The renv cycle](#sec-renv-cycle) - [What the lockfile records](#sec-renv-lockfile) - [Keeping the lockfile honest](#sec-renv-honest) - [Worked example: a project's lifecycle](#sec-renv-worked) - [renv inside a container](#sec-renv-docker) ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Skip ahead?'} If these answers come quickly, skip to the next chapter. The answers are in @sec-quiz-answers-08. 1. What does `renv::init()` do to a project directory, and what new files does it create? 2. What is stored in `renv.lock`, and why is the lock file version-controlled while `renv/library/` is not? 3. What is the difference between `renv::snapshot()` and `renv::restore()`? ::: ## The renv cycle {#sec-renv-cycle} `renv` [@ushey2026renv] succeeded `packrat`, now deprecated, and is maintained by Posit; it is the standard for project-level R package management. There are only three verbs to learn, and they behave exactly as documented. What `renv` cannot decide is when to use them, and a lockfile snapshotted at the wrong moments records a history nobody can read. ### Initializing a project ```r # in a new or existing project renv::init() ``` `init()` creates the files in @tbl-renv-files. It also writes `renv/.gitignore`, which keeps the library out of Git. | File | Role | Committed? | |---|---|---| | `renv.lock` | The lockfile: every package's version and source | Yes | | `.Rprofile` | Runs `source("renv/activate.R")` at session start | Yes | | `renv/activate.R` | The bootstrap script that activates the project library | Yes | | `renv/settings.json` | Project-specific `renv` settings | Yes | | `renv/library/` | The project library of installed packages | No | : The files `renv::init()` creates. {#tbl-renv-files} The `.Rprofile` bootstrap is the right default: it ensures that collaborators get the project library without thinking about it. Disable it only for a specific reason, such as a shared server project where users deliberately run different package versions. After `init()`, `.libPaths()` returns the project library first, so `install.packages("dplyr")` installs into the project's library, not your global one. On macOS the result looks like this (display-only; paths vary by machine): ```r .libPaths() #> [1] "/path/to/project/renv/library/macos/R-4.4/x86_64" #> [2] "/Users/you/Library/Caches/org.R-project.R/R/renv/sandbox/..." ``` The second entry is the *sandbox*: a read-only library holding only R's base and recommended packages, which keeps packages from your global library out of the project. The package *cache* does not appear in `.libPaths()` at all; it sits behind the project library, which links to it, and it is shared across projects on the same machine, so installing a package another project already has is fast. ### Snapshot and restore The two verbs at the center of `renv` move in opposite directions across the same boundary, as @fig-renv-cycle shows. `snapshot()` reads the state of your project library and writes it to `renv.lock`; `restore()` reads `renv.lock` and rebuilds the library to match. The lockfile is the durable record that travels in Git; the library is the disposable build product it regenerates. ```{mermaid} %%| echo: false %%| label: fig-renv-cycle %%| fig-alt: "Two nodes in a cycle. The project library of installed %%| packages feeds renv.lock through renv::snapshot(), and %%| renv.lock rebuilds the project library through %%| renv::restore(). Only renv.lock is marked as versioned in %%| Git." %%| fig-cap: "The renv cycle. snapshot() records the project library %%| into the lockfile; restore() rebuilds the library from the %%| lockfile. Only the lockfile is committed to Git." flowchart LR L["Project library
installed packages"] -->|"renv::snapshot()"| F["renv.lock
versioned in Git"] F -->|"renv::restore()"| L ``` The core workflow (display-only, because it changes a project library): ```r install.packages("ggplot2") renv::snapshot() # then, in the shell: # git add renv.lock && git commit -m "Add ggplot2" ``` `renv::snapshot()` finds the packages your code references, by the static scan described in @sec-renv-honest, looks up the versions installed in the project library, and updates `renv.lock`. To recreate the environment elsewhere, clone the repository and run: ```r renv::restore() ``` This installs exactly the recorded versions into the project library. The first restore takes a while (downloads and builds); later restores reuse the cache. Snapshot at meaningful moments, not after every `install.packages()`: at project start, when a dependency intentionally changes, and before each submission. A snapshot after every install produces noisy commits, and the lockfile's Git history is the story of the project's dependencies; keep it readable. ### Reading `status()` `renv::status()` compares three things (the packages your code uses, the project library, and the lockfile) and reports where they disagree. Each report has a direction, and the resolution depends on which side is the truth. | `status()` reports | What it means | Usual resolution | |---|---|---| | Installed version differs from recorded | The library or the lockfile changed since the last snapshot | `snapshot()` if you upgraded deliberately; `restore()` if the lockfile is the truth, as on a fresh clone | | Used but not installed | Code calls a package the library lacks | `renv::install()`, then `snapshot()` | | Installed and used but not recorded | A snapshot was forgotten | `snapshot()` | | Recorded but no longer used | The code dropped a dependency | `snapshot()`, which removes it | : Reading `renv::status()`. {#tbl-renv-status} ::: {.callout-important title='LLM prompt'} Use a model to explain an unfamiliar `status()` report, not to choose the direction for you. > **Context.** Below are the output of `renv::status()` and of > `git log -3 --stat -- renv.lock` for an R analysis project. I > [cloned the repository today | upgraded `dplyr` on purpose > yesterday]. > > **Constraints.** Do not suggest `renv::update()`, removing > `renv.lock`, or reinstalling everything. Recommend one `renv` > command per flagged package. > > **Criteria.** For each flagged package, say which side (library > or lockfile) is the truth and why, citing my situation above. > State what `git diff renv.lock` should show after your command. *Failure mode.* Models confuse the direction: `restore()` after a deliberate upgrade silently downgrades the package, and `snapshot()` on a fresh clone overwrites a collaborator's lockfile with whatever your machine happens to have. *Check.* Run `renv::status()` again, which should report no issues, and read `git diff renv.lock`, which should change only the packages you meant to change. A status report and a lockfile hold package names and versions, not data, so they may go to any approved tool (@sec-ai-governance). ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'} **Question.** You install `dplyr` 1.1.4 in your project, work for a week, then notice the lockfile still records 1.1.0. What happens if you `restore()` instead of `snapshot()`? **Answer.** `restore()` reads the lockfile and installs *that* version, so it downgrades `dplyr` from 1.1.4 to 1.1.0. To keep 1.1.4, `snapshot()` instead, which updates the lockfile to match what you have installed. Snapshot writes from library to lockfile; restore writes from lockfile to library. The disagreement `status()` flags means you have to decide which direction to go: restore when the lockfile is the truth (a fresh clone), snapshot when the library is the truth (a deliberate upgrade). ::: ## What the lockfile records {#sec-renv-lockfile} ### Anatomy of `renv.lock` The lockfile is JSON (JavaScript Object Notation): plain text, version-controlled, and readable by people and programs. `renv::lockfile_read()` parses it into an R list. The chunk below reads the lockfile that pins the environment this book was built in. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} lock <- renv::lockfile_read("../../renv.lock") lock$R$Version #> [1] "4.6.1" length(lock$Packages) #> [1] 215 table(vapply(lock$Packages, \(p) p$Source, character(1))) #> #> GitHub Repository #> 1 214 str(lock$Packages$dplyr[c("Package", "Version", "Source", "Repository")]) #> List of 4 #> $ Package : chr "dplyr" #> $ Version : chr "1.2.1" #> $ Source : chr "Repository" #> $ Repository: chr "CRAN" ``` ::: The fields that matter: | Field | Meaning | |---|---| | `R$Version` | The R version the lockfile was written under (recorded, not installed) | | `Version` | The package version to install | | `Source` | Where the package came from: `Repository` (CRAN, the Comprehensive R Archive Network, or Bioconductor), `GitHub`, `Bitbucket`, or local | | `Repository` | Which repository, for `Source: Repository` | | `RemoteSha` | For a GitHub package, the exact commit installed | : Lockfile fields. {#tbl-renv-fields} Lockfiles written by earlier versions of `renv` also carry a `Hash` field, which `renv` uses to identify an installation in its cache; the lockfile above has none. The lockfile stores names, versions, and sources, never binaries, so it is portable between macOS and Linux by construction: each machine builds or downloads the binaries appropriate to its own architecture. ### Which packages it records What you choose is *which* packages the lockfile records, through the `type` argument of `renv::snapshot()`: | `type` | Records | Use when | |---|---|---| | `"implicit"` (default) | Packages `renv::dependencies()` finds in your code, with their dependencies | Scripts and research compendia | | `"explicit"` | Only packages declared in `DESCRIPTION` | The compendium's `DESCRIPTION` is complete and maintained | | `"all"` | Everything in the project library | Rarely; it includes packages you tried once and abandoned | : Snapshot types. {#tbl-renv-snapshot-types} ### Packages from GitHub and Bioconductor Some packages live outside CRAN, and `renv` installs them by the same verbs (display-only): ```r renv::install("benmarwick/rrtools") renv::install("bioc::DESeq2") renv::snapshot() ``` The lockfile records the source (the GitHub commit, or the Bioconductor release), and `restore()` reinstalls from the same source. For GitHub packages the pin is exact: later commits to the repository do not reach your project unless you upgrade deliberately. The book's own lockfile holds one GitHub package: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} zz <- lock$Packages$zzpower zz[grep("^(Package|Version|Source|Remote)", names(zz))] |> str() #> List of 9 #> $ Package : chr "zzpower" #> $ Version : chr "1.1.0" #> $ Source : chr "GitHub" #> $ RemoteType : chr "github" #> $ RemoteHost : chr "api.github.com" #> $ RemoteUsername: chr "rgt47" #> $ RemoteRepo : chr "zzpower" #> $ RemoteRef : chr "main" #> $ RemoteSha : chr "517ceb6ec67cee7b1f28cf702297f7d2baef047f" ``` ::: ::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'} Confirm that every GitHub package in your lockfile is pinned to a full commit SHA (secure hash algorithm, a 40-character hexadecimal identifier), not only to a branch name. Run from your project root: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} github <- Filter(\(p) identical(p$Source, "GitHub"), lock$Packages) shas <- vapply(github, \(p) p$RemoteSha %||% NA_character_, character(1)) stopifnot(all(grepl("^[0-9a-f]{40}$", shas))) shas #> zzpower #> "517ceb6ec67cee7b1f28cf702297f7d2baef047f" ``` ::: In your own project, replace `"../../renv.lock"` above with `"renv.lock"`. ::: ### Exercises 1. Add a GitHub-sourced package to your project (`renv::install('user/repo')`), snapshot, and check that the lockfile captures the commit SHA. (This modifies your project library and lockfile.) ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'} `renv::lockfile_read("renv.lock")$Packages$$RemoteSha` returns a 40-character hexadecimal string, and `RemoteRef` names the branch or tag it came from. If `RemoteSha` is missing, the package was installed some other way (for example with `remotes` outside the project library); reinstall it with `renv::install()` and snapshot again. The Verification above is the general form of this check. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'} **Question.** A colleague on Linux restores your lockfile, written on a Mac. Does the lockfile give them your binaries, and does it give them your R version? **Answer.** Neither. The lockfile records package names, versions, and sources, and each machine builds or downloads its own binaries, which is why the same lockfile works on both systems. It records your R version in `R$Version` but does not install it; a colleague on a different R gets your package versions on their interpreter. Pinning R itself is the container's job (@sec-renv-docker). ::: ## Keeping the lockfile honest {#sec-renv-honest} A lockfile is only as good as the moments at which it was written. Three practices keep it an accurate record: upgrade deliberately, make sure it contains everything the code loads, and audit it before you tag a release. ### Upgrading deliberately `renv` does not update your packages unless you ask, which is a feature. When a security fix or a useful feature appears, upgrade one package deliberately, re-run the analysis, compare the results with the previous run, then snapshot and commit. Resist upgrading everything at once: if a number moves, you then cannot say which package moved it. ::: {.callout-warning title='Pitfall'} **A snapshot after an unreviewed upgrade records the regression as the new truth.** Running `update.packages()` or `renv::update()` and then `renv::snapshot()` without re-running the analysis is exactly the January-to-July failure: the lockfile now pins the versions that changed the number, and the old versions survive only in Git history. Compare the results before you snapshot. ::: Restoring an old lockfile years later raises a second problem: the recorded versions may now be available only as source, which must be compiled. Posit Public Package Manager (P3M) serves CRAN as it stood on any given date, with prebuilt Linux binaries. Pointing the project's repository at a dated snapshot (display-only) makes installs and restores reproducible against that date:[^p3m] ```r options(repos = c( CRAN = "https://packagemanager.posit.co/cran/2026-01-15" )) renv::snapshot() ``` [^p3m]: The URL pattern, with the date as the last component, is as of 2026-10. The Linux binary URLs add a distribution segment; the P3M setup page for your operating system gives the exact form. ### Migrating an existing project For a project that has been using packages without `renv`, run `renv::init()` from inside it. `init()` calls `renv::dependencies()`, which scans the project's R, R Markdown, and Quarto files *statically*, without running them, for `library()`, `require()`, `requireNamespace()`, and `pkg::fn()` calls, installs what it finds, and writes an initial lockfile. If the project has a `DESCRIPTION` file with `Imports:` declarations, `renv` uses those as well. Because the scan does not run the code, it misses packages loaded indirectly. The chunk below builds a three-line toy project in a temporary directory and scans it. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} toy <- file.path(tempdir(), "toy-project") dir.create(file.path(toy, "R"), recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE) writeLines(c( "library(dplyr)", "fit <- survival::coxph(survival::Surv(time, status) ~ age,", " data = survival::lung)", "plot_pkg <- \"ggplot2\"", "library(plot_pkg, character.only = TRUE)" ), file.path(toy, "R", "analysis.R")) found <- renv::dependencies(toy, progress = FALSE) unique(found$Package) #> [1] "dplyr" "survival" setdiff(c("dplyr", "survival", "ggplot2"), found$Package) #> [1] "ggplot2" ``` ::: The scan finds `dplyr` and `survival` and misses `ggplot2`, whose name is held in a variable. A lockfile built from this scan would omit it, and a collaborator's `restore()` would succeed and then the script would fail at the `library()` call. ::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'} List every indirectly loaded package as a plain `library()` call in a `_dependencies.R` file at the project root, then re-scan and assert that nothing the code needs is missing. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} writeLines("library(ggplot2)", file.path(toy, "_dependencies.R")) found <- renv::dependencies(toy, progress = FALSE) stopifnot(all(c("dplyr", "survival", "ggplot2") %in% found$Package)) unique(found$Package) #> [1] "ggplot2" "dplyr" "survival" ``` ::: In your own project, run `renv::dependencies()` and compare its list with the packages you know the analysis loads, then run the analysis once from a fresh session. ::: ### Auditing before submission Before a project is submitted for publication or deposited (for example to Zenodo), audit it with the community tools first. `renv::status()` confirms that the library and the lockfile agree and that every package the code uses is recorded (@tbl-renv-status); `renv::dependencies()` lists what the code loads. Together they catch the common drift: a forgotten `snapshot()`, a package added without a lockfile update, and a colleague's machine that ran `update.packages()` outside `renv`. One way to automate part of the audit is the in-house `zzrenvcheck` package (@sec-lab-software), which `zzcollab` projects run through `make check-renv` (@sec-zzcollab). Its `check_packages()` compares the code against `DESCRIPTION` and, separately, `DESCRIPTION` against `renv.lock`; by default it does not include indirect dependencies, so it can report success while `renv::status()` still lists packages missing from the lockfile, and it does not flag a locked package nothing uses. It reads files only and never inspects the installed library, so it is a narrower, faster check to run often, not a replacement for `renv::status()`, which remains the authority before a release. ```r zzrenvcheck::check_packages() ``` Resolve every issue `check_packages()` reports, then run `renv::status()` to confirm; it checks more than `zzrenvcheck` does. ### Exercises 2. Run `renv::status()` and `renv::dependencies()` on a project of yours and fix any disagreement they report; if the project uses `zzcollab`, also run `zzrenvcheck::check_packages()`. (This modifies your project; `renv::status()` is the verification.) ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'} A clean result is `renv::status()` reporting that no issues were found, and a `renv::dependencies()` list that contains every package you know the analysis loads. Each fix should appear as a small, readable change in `git diff renv.lock`. A diff that changes dozens of versions means a snapshot recorded an upgrade you did not intend; revert it and upgrade one package at a time. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'} **Question.** In the toy project, why does the static scan miss `ggplot2`, and why is the failure that follows only *eventually* loud? **Answer.** `renv::dependencies()` reads the source without running it, so it sees `library(plot_pkg, character.only = TRUE)` but cannot know that `plot_pkg` holds `"ggplot2"`. On your machine nothing fails, because `ggplot2` is already installed. The failure appears only when someone restores the lockfile on a clean machine and runs the script, possibly months later and after the analysis has been reported. The `_dependencies.R` file makes it loud now. ::: ## Worked example: a project's lifecycle {#sec-renv-worked} The lifecycle below is display-only, because each step changes a project library. It shows when each verb runs over a project's life. ```r # day 1: start the project renv::init() install.packages(c("dplyr", "ggplot2")) renv::snapshot() # git add renv.lock && git commit -m "Initial deps" # week 4: add a new dependency install.packages("survival") renv::snapshot() # git add renv.lock && git commit -m "Add survival" # week 8: upgrade dplyr deliberately, and compare before recording saveRDS(results, "before-upgrade.rds") install.packages("dplyr") renv::status() # re-run the analysis, then: all.equal(readRDS("before-upgrade.rds"), results) renv::snapshot() # git add renv.lock && git commit -m "Upgrade dplyr to 1.1.4" # week 12: a collaborator clones the repository renv::restore() ``` At submission, tag the commit from the shell: ```bash git tag -a v1.0-submission \ -m "Submitted to journal; renv.lock pins R 4.4.0, dplyr 1.1.4" git push origin v1.0-submission ``` The lockfile evolves through the project's life, recording each dependency change as a commit, and the tag captures the exact environment at submission for later reproduction. ::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'} Confirm that the tag carries the lockfile you think it does, and that the working library matches it: ```bash git show v1.0-submission:renv.lock | head -n 4 Rscript -e 'renv::status()' ``` The first command prints the start of the lockfile as of the tag, including its R version; the second should report no issues. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'} **Question.** In week 8, `all.equal()` reports that one estimate differs in the fourth decimal place. What do you do before `snapshot()`? **Answer.** Find out why before recording anything. Read the upgraded package's NEWS for a changed default or a fixed bug, and decide whether the new number is a correction or a regression. If it is a correction, snapshot, commit, and say in the commit message what changed and why; if it is a regression, `restore()` returns the library to the recorded version. Either way the decision is recorded, which is the point of the lockfile. ::: ## renv inside a container {#sec-renv-docker} `renv` pins R packages. It does not pin R itself, the system libraries that packages link to, or the operating system, so the book pairs it with Docker in @sec-docker. The part of a Dockerfile that belongs to `renv` is four lines; the full file, with a digest-pinned base image and a `.dockerignore`, is in @sec-docker-canonical. ```dockerfile COPY renv.lock .Rprofile ./ COPY renv/activate.R renv/activate.R RUN R -q -e "renv::restore(prompt = FALSE)" COPY . . ``` The order matters. Docker caches each layer, so copying the lockfile and its two small bootstrap files *before* the project means that edits to the project do not invalidate the slow package-installation layer. Only a change to `renv.lock` (or to the bootstrap files) rebuilds it, which is correct: when dependencies change, the layer should rebuild. ::: {.callout-important title='LLM prompt'} > **Context.** My project's `renv.lock` records R > ``. The > analysis renders with `quarto render analysis/paper/paper.qmd`. > > **Constraints.** Base the image on `rocker/r-ver` at the tag equal > to that R version, pinned by digest. Copy `renv.lock`, > `.Rprofile`, and `renv/activate.R` and run > `renv::restore(prompt = FALSE)` before copying the rest of the > project. Write a `.dockerignore` that excludes `renv/library/`, > `.Renviron`, and `.git/`. > > **Criteria.** The image builds; after I edit a `.qmd` file and > rebuild, the restore step is reported as cached; inside the > container, `R --version` matches the lockfile and > `renv::status()` reports no issues. *Failure mode.* The model writes a base-image tag from its training data, such as `rocker/r-ver:4.4.0` or `latest`, that does not match your lockfile, or copies the whole project before the restore, so that every edit reinstalls every package. *Check.* Build twice with an edit in between and look for the cached restore step, then run `renv::status()` inside the container. Compare the draft with @sec-docker-canonical. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'} **Question.** Your project has a committed `renv.lock` pinning every package to an exact version. A colleague clones it and runs `renv::restore()`. Are you guaranteed the same numbers? **Answer.** No, and what is left over is the reason this book puts Docker in the next chapter rather than stopping here. `renv` pins R packages. It does not pin: - **R itself.** The lockfile records the R version but does not install it. - **System libraries.** Packages that link to GDAL (the Geospatial Data Abstraction Library), GSL (the GNU Scientific Library), or a specific BLAS (Basic Linear Algebra Subprograms) behave differently against different system versions, and none of that is in the lockfile. A different BLAS can change the last digits of a regression coefficient. - **The operating system**, and anything that depends on locale, line endings, or file-system case sensitivity. So `renv::restore()` gets you the same *package* versions, which removes the largest and most common source of drift, but not the same computational environment. That is the division of labor between the Five Pillars (Dockerfile, `renv.lock`, `.Rprofile`, source code, and data, defined in @sec-zzcollab): `renv.lock` handles the R layer and the Dockerfile handles everything beneath it. Either alone leaves a gap, which is why the pillars are a stack rather than a menu. ::: ### Exercises 3. Write a Dockerfile that restores your project's `renv.lock`. Build it, and verify that the package versions inside the container match the lockfile. ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'} Start from the canonical Dockerfile in @sec-docker-canonical. Inside the container, `Rscript -e 'renv::status()'` should report no issues, and `R --version` should print the version in the lockfile's `R$Version`. If `status()` lists packages as not installed, the restore layer failed partway, usually for a missing system library; the build log names it. ::: ## Rules of thumb 1. **Habit 4: pin the environment.** Snapshot writes the lockfile, restore reads it, and a container pins what the lockfile cannot. 2. **Habit 3: version control from day one.** Commit `renv.lock` with the change that needed it, and tag the commit you submit. 3. **Habit 8: a plausible number is the expensive bug.** Upgrade one package at a time and compare the results before you snapshot. ## Cumulative practice 4. *Cumulative (uses @sec-git-solo).* Initialize `renv` in an existing project of yours and commit the lockfile. Clone the project into a new directory (or a Docker container) and run `renv::restore()`. Verify that the scripts produce identical output, for example by comparing saved results with `all.equal()`. 5. *On your own work (no key).* Migrate a project of yours that does not use `renv` to `renv`. Document the steps, every package the dependency scan missed, and any other issues you met. ## Cheat sheet | Verb | Direction | When | |---|---|---| | `renv::init()` | Creates the project library and first lockfile | Once, at project start or migration | | `renv::install("pkg")` | Installs into the project library (CRAN, `user/repo`, `bioc::pkg`) | Adding or upgrading a package | | `renv::snapshot()` | Library to lockfile | After a deliberate change; before submission | | `renv::restore()` | Lockfile to library | After cloning; to undo an unintended change | | `renv::status()` | Compares code, library, and lockfile | Before every commit of `renv.lock` and every tag | | `renv::dependencies()` | Scans code for packages | Migration; auditing for missed packages | | `renv::lockfile_read()` | Reads the lockfile into R | Inspecting versions and sources | | `git show :renv.lock` | Retrieves the lockfile at a tag | Reproducing a submitted analysis | : The `renv` verbs card. {#tbl-renv-cheat-sheet} ## Further reading - [@ushey2026renv], the `renv` package and its documentation, the definitive reference. - The `renv` CRAN vignettes, starting with 'Introduction to renv'. - Posit's *Reproducible environments* technical guide. ## Prerequisites answers {#sec-quiz-answers-08} 1. `renv::init()` creates an `renv/` subdirectory (with an `activate.R` bootstrap script), an `.Rprofile` that calls it, and an initial `renv.lock`. From then on the project uses a private library isolated from the user's global library; `install.packages()` installs into the project library, not the user library. 2. `renv.lock` is a JSON file listing the R version and the exact package versions and sources used by the project. It is plain text and is version-controlled. The `renv/library/` directory contains the actual installed binaries, which are large, platform-specific, and reproducible from the lockfile, so they are kept out of Git. The lockfile is the portable specification; the library is a local build product. 3. `renv::snapshot()` finds the packages your code uses, reads their installed versions from the project library, and writes them into `renv.lock`. You call it after installing a new package or upgrading. `renv::restore()` reads `renv.lock` and installs exactly those packages into the project library. You call it after cloning a project on a new machine. Snapshot writes from library to lockfile; restore writes from lockfile to library.
